subject: KLUGE (1964)
object: KLUGE (1964) reported on familial cancer of the colon.

subject: Lovett (1976)
object: Lovett (1976) took family histories from 209 patients being treated for cancer of the colon or rectum at St Mark's Hospital and obtained death certificates for parents and sibs who had died. Among these relatives, deaths from bowel cancer were more than three times the number expected for a comparable group from the general population.

subject: Lovett (1976)
object: Lovett (1976) identified three features of an index case that were associated with a higher likelihood that other family members had also had cancer of the large bowel: multiple benign or malignant tumors in the large bowel, a history of a previous primary carcinoma or adenoma of the large bowel, and early age of onset of bowel carcinoma.

subject: Lovett (1976)
object: Lovett (1976) described a family with a high incidence of early-onset gastrointestinal carcinoma, with affected individuals proven in four generations. The management of unaffected family members was discussed and a follow-up regimen was suggested.

subject: Williams (1978)
object: Williams (1978) described a further 'cancer family' and recommended that cancer patients from such families receive careful lifelong follow-up. Williams (1978) also recommended that all members of cancer families be screened for cancer of the uterus and colon and be taught methods of cancer detection and the importance of early diagnosis.

subject: Perucho et al. (1981)
object: Perucho et al. (1981) transfected DNA from cultured human tumor cell lines into NIH/3T3 mouse cells and looked for transformed foci. They concluded that 5 of the lines contained a gene or genes able to transform mouse cells, and that at least 3 different transforming genes were present among these 5 lines. Three of the lines, 2 from lung carcinomas and 1 from a colon carcinoma, transferred the same or closely related human genes. The authors suggested that, if these genes were mediating tumorigenesis, overlapping pathways leading to tumorigenesis may arise independently.

subject: Sivak et al. (1981)
object: Sivak et al. (1981) reported a kindred with the familial cancer syndrome in which every confirmed affected member had at least one primary carcinoma of the colon. The average age at which cancer appeared was 38 years, and 23% of the cancer patients had multiple primary neoplasms. Colonoscopy found no unsuspected cancers in family members at risk.

subject: Sivak et al. (1981)
object: Sivak et al. (1981) found that transmission of the cancer trait in their colon cancer kindred was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

subject: Sivak et al. (1981)
object: Sivak et al. (1981) performed HLA typing in a kindred with inherited colon adenocarcinoma, with data from direct typing or inference available for 66 living and deceased individuals. In the offspring of 4 informative matings there were only 3 crossovers out of a possible 17, and the total lod score was 1.06 at a recombination fraction of 0.20.

subject: Budd and Fink (1981)
object: Budd and Fink (1981) described a family in which 17 members across 3 generations had cancers. Fourteen had adenocarcinoma of the colon, mostly the mucoid variant. Other tumors in the family were endometrial adenocarcinoma, atypical endometrial hyperplasia, uterine leiomyosarcoma, transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder, and renal cell carcinoma.

subject: Budd and Fink (1981)
object: Budd and Fink (1981) concluded that the mucoid colonic carcinoma syndrome in this 3-generation family was inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. They suggested that the defective autosomal locus was pleiotropic, causing several types of extracolonic cancer.

subject: Bamezai et al. (1984)
object: Bamezai et al. (1984) described a nonconsanguineous Indian Sikh kindred of 46 individuals in which 8 had site-specific colon (caecum) cancer not associated with polyposis. The authors considered the clinical features indicative of a 'cancer family syndrome.'

subject: Bamezai et al. (1984)
object: Bamezai et al. (1984) found that site-specific colon cancer in an Indian Sikh kindred showed an autosomal dominant transmission pattern, probably with 100% penetrance. They suggested the responsible gene may have arisen by germline mutation in the first generation and remained heterozygous in affected individuals.

subject: Bamezai et al. (1984)
object: Bamezai et al. (1984) observed a low mitotic index and no structural or numerical chromosomal aberrations in the 2 probands available for study from a kindred with site-specific colon cancer.

subject: Burt et al. (1985)
object: Burt et al. (1985) studied a large Utah pedigree that had multiple cases of common colorectal cancer but no recognizable inheritance pattern. Pedigree members and spouse controls were screened with flexible proctosigmoidoscopy. One or more adenomatous polyps were found in 21% of family members (41 of 191), compared with 9% of controls (12 of 132) (P less than 0.005).

subject: Burt et al. (1985)
object: Burt et al. (1985) used likelihood methods to compare random occurrence of cancer and polyps with autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant inheritance in the Utah pedigree. The analysis suggested that the excess of discrete adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancers was caused by an inherited autosomal dominant susceptibility gene, rather than a recessive gene or chance. The authors suggested that this type of inheritance may be more common than previously recognized.

subject: Pathak and Goodacre (1986)
object: Pathak and Goodacre (1986) suggested that a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 12 was a specific abnormality in a limited number of colorectal carcinoma samples. They proposed that fragile sites expressed at these specific chromosomal regions in normal peripheral blood cultures might identify individuals predisposed to develop a particular type of neoplasm.

subject: Mecklin (1987)
object: Mecklin (1987) studied all 468 colorectal carcinoma patients diagnosed in one Finnish county (0.25 million inhabitants) from 1970 to 1979 and found that the cancer family syndrome type of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal carcinoma was the most common verifiable risk factor, involving 3.8 to 5.5% of patients. The frequencies of familial adenomatosis and ulcerative colitis were 0.2% and 0.6%, respectively. Because diagnosis relied on family history with cancer in 2 or more generations, the author suggested that the observed frequency of 4 to 6% for the syndrome may be an underestimate.

subject: Mecklin (1987)
object: Mecklin (1987) found that patients with cancer family syndrome were young, accounting for 29 to 39% of colorectal carcinoma patients under 50 years of age, and that their tumors were located predominantly (65%) in the right hemicolon. The author concluded that the high frequency of hereditary cases indicated the importance of taking the family history of every new patient.

subject: Fearon et al. (1987)
object: Fearon et al. (1987) used X-linked RFLPs to study X chromosome inactivation in colorectal tumors from females. All 50 tumors examined, 20 carcinomas and 30 adenomas of either familial or spontaneous type, had monoclonal inactivation patterns. The authors concluded that this supported a monoclonal origin for colorectal neoplasms.

subject: Fearon et al. (1987)
object: Fearon et al. (1987) used autosomal RFLPs as clonal markers. They found somatic loss of chromosome 17p sequences in more than 75% of the colorectal carcinomas examined, but such loss was rare in adenomas. The authors suggested that a gene on 17p may be associated with progression from the benign to the malignant state.

subject: Bos et al. (1987)
object: Bos et al. (1987) combined DNA hybridization analyses with tissue sectioning techniques and found ras gene mutations in over a third of human colorectal cancers. Most of the mutations were at codon 12 of the c-Ki-ras (KRAS) gene.

subject: KRAS codon 12 of the c-Ki-ras gene
object: KRAS

subject: Bos et al. (1987)
object: Bos et al. (1987) concluded that ras gene mutations in colorectal tumors usually occur before malignancy develops. This suggested that they are an early event in colorectal tumor development.

subject: Okamoto et al. (1988)
object: Okamoto et al. (1988) used polymorphic DNA markers to look for somatic loss of heterozygosity in 38 tumors from 25 patients with familial polyposis coli and in 20 sporadic colon carcinomas from 19 patients. Allele loss on chromosome 22 was frequent, with some additional losses on chromosomes 5, 6, 12q, and 15. The authors suggested that more than one chromosomal locus may be involved in the development of familial and sporadic colon carcinomas.

subject: Okamoto et al. (1988)
object: Okamoto et al. (1988) found frequent allele loss with C11p11, a DNA probe linked to the familial polyposis coli gene, in both familial and sporadic colon carcinomas. They did not find this loss in benign adenomas.

subject: Vogelstein et al. (1988)
object: Vogelstein et al. (1988) looked for ras-gene mutations and allelic deletions of chromosomes 5, 17, and 18 in 172 colorectal tumor specimens representing different stages of neoplasia: 40 predominantly early-stage adenomas from 7 patients with familial adenomatous polyposis, 40 adenomas from 33 patients without polyposis, and 92 carcinomas from 89 patients. Ras-gene mutations occurred in 58% of adenomas larger than 1 cm and 47% of carcinomas, but in only 9% of adenomas under 1 cm.

subject: Vogelstein et al. (1988)
object: Vogelstein et al. (1988) found that chromosome 5 sequences linked to the familial adenomatous polyposis gene were not lost in adenomas from polyposis patients but were lost in 29 to 35% of adenomas and carcinomas from other patients. A specific region of chromosome 18 was deleted in 73% of carcinomas and 47% of advanced adenomas but in only 11 to 13% of earlier-stage adenomas, and chromosome 17p sequences were usually lost only in carcinomas (75%).

subject: Vogelstein et al. (1988)
object: Vogelstein et al. (1988) found that the four molecular alterations accumulated in a fashion paralleling the clinical progression of colorectal tumors, consistent with a model in which development of cancer often involves mutational activation of an oncogene coupled with loss of several tumor suppressor genes.

subject: Cannon-Albright et al. (1988)
object: Cannon-Albright et al. (1988) studied 670 persons in 34 kindreds by flexible proctosigmoidoscopy; kindreds were ascertained through a single person with an adenomatous polyp or a cluster of relatives with colon cancer, and had common colorectal cancer rather than familial polyposis coli or nonpolyposis inherited colorectal cancer. Likelihood analysis strongly supported dominant inheritance of susceptibility to colorectal adenomas and cancers, with a gene frequency of 19%. Under the most likely model, adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancers occurred only in genetically susceptible persons (95% CI for this proportion, 53 to 100%).

subject: Cannon-Albright et al. (1988)
object: Cannon-Albright et al. (1988) suggested that an inherited susceptibility to colonic adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancer is common (estimated gene frequency 19%) and is responsible for the majority of clinically observed colonic neoplasms, and that genetic and environmental factors interact in polyp formation and transformation; they supported screening of first-degree relatives of colorectal cancer patients.

subject: Law et al. (1988)
object: Law et al. (1988) studied allelic loss in colorectal carcinomas. To get purer tumor samples, they microdissected tumor cells from 24 carcinomas, engrafted 9 more in nude mice, and flow-sorted nuclei from 2 others. Loss of heterozygosity was found for chromosome 5 alleles in 6 of 31 informative cancers (19%), for chromosome 17 in 19 of 34 (56%), and for chromosome 18 in 17 of 33 (52%).

subject: Law et al. (1988)
object: Law et al. (1988) concluded that the familial polyposis coli gene on chromosome 5 appears to act as a true dominant for adenomatosis but not as a common recessive gene for colon cancer. They also suggested that simple Mendelian models in which alleles are lost at a single locus may not be suitable for understanding common human solid tumors.

subject: Wildrick and Boman (1988)
object: Wildrick and Boman (1988) compared matched normal and tumor DNA from patients with sporadic colon carcinoma using a probe for the glucocorticoid receptor (GRL) locus on 5q11-q13. This locus lies close to one of two proposed sites of a constitutional deletion seen in a patient with familial adenomatous polyposis. At least 27% of tumors showed tumor-specific allele loss at GRL. The authors concluded that this supports the hypothesis that hereditary and sporadic forms of colon cancer result from mutations of the same gene.

subject: Vogelstein et al. (1989)
object: Vogelstein et al. (1989) studied polymorphic DNA markers from every nonacrocentric autosomal arm in 56 paired colorectal carcinoma and adjacent normal colonic mucosa specimens. They called this analysis an 'allelotype.' Allelic deletions were very common: for every polymorphic marker tested, one allele was lost in at least some tumors, and some tumors lost more than half of their parental alleles.

subject: Vogelstein et al. (1989)
object: Vogelstein et al. (1989) found new DNA fragments that were absent from normal tissue in 5 of 56 colorectal carcinomas. These new fragments contained repeated sequences of the variable number of tandem repeat (VNTR) type.

subject: Vogelstein et al. (1989)
object: Vogelstein et al. (1989) found that patients whose colorectal carcinomas had more than the median percentage of allelic deletions had a considerably worse prognosis than the other patients, even though primary tumor size and stage were very similar in the two groups. The authors suggested that tumor allelotype may provide a molecular tool for better estimating prognosis in colorectal cancer.

subject: Delattre et al. (1989)
object: Delattre et al. (1989) investigated multiple genetic alterations in colorectal cancers, including changes in DNA content, ras oncogene mutations, and deletions involving chromosomes 5, 17, and 18. Deletions and mitotic abnormalities were both significantly more frequent in distal than in proximal tumors, and deletions were significantly associated with each other and with change in DNA content.

subject: Delattre et al. (1989)
object: Delattre et al. (1989) found that the frequency of somatic c-Ki-ras mutations in colorectal cancer did not differ between proximal and distal tumors.

subject: Delattre et al. (1989)
object: Delattre et al. (1989) concluded that their data strongly supported the hypothesis that proximal and distal colon carcinomas might differ in the genetic mechanisms underlying their initiation and/or progression.

subject: Fearon and Vogelstein (1990)
object: Fearon and Vogelstein (1990) proposed a genetic model for colorectal tumorigenesis.

subject: Konstantinova et al. (1991)
object: Konstantinova et al. (1991) analyzed chromosome abnormalities in 15 colorectal tumors. Rearrangements of 17p leading to deletion of the arm or part of it were found in 12 tumors, and loss of one chromosome 17 homolog in 2 others; loss of chromosome 18 was found in 12 of 13 cases with fully identified numerical abnormalities. Other losses involved chromosome 5 (6 tumors), 21 (5), and 4, 15, and 22 (4 each); gains included extra copies of chromosome 20 (6 tumors), 8q (5), and 13q (6), and rearrangements of 1p and 11q were each found in 6 tumors.

subject: Konstantinova et al. (1991)
object: Konstantinova et al. (1991) noted that, unlike other series, their colorectal tumors showed a high frequency of sex chromosome loss (X missing in 4 of 7 tumors from females; Y absent in 5 of 8 tumors from males) and rearrangements of 9q in 8 cases, with the breakpoint at 9q22 in 5. Cytologic signs of gene amplification (double minutes or multiple microchromosomes) were seen in 6 tumors.

subject: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992)
object: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992) looked for p53 mutations and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) in 274 colorectal tumors of 4 histopathologic grades. In 160 tumors from 40 patients with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), p53 mutations were found in 0 of 58 adenomas with moderate dysplasia, 3 of 37 severe adenomas, 6 of 40 intramucosal carcinomas, and 10 of 25 invasive carcinomas. Both mutation and LOH were seen in 1 of 33 severe adenomas, 6 of 24 intramucosal carcinomas, and 10 of 25 invasive carcinomas. Every intramucosal and invasive carcinoma with a mutation had lost the other p53 allele.

subject: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992)
object: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992) obtained similar results in 114 tumors from 86 patients without FAP. No adenoma had both a p53 mutation and LOH, but both changes were present in intramucosal and invasive carcinomas.

subject: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992)
object: Of the 56 p53 mutations that Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992) found, the codons most often affected were 175, 238, 245, 248, 273, and 282; 4 of these codons encode arginine. GC-to-AT transitions made up 39 of 54 mutations (72%).

subject: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992)
object: Kikuchi-Yanoshita et al. (1992) found high p53 polyadenylated RNA expression in every invasive carcinoma, whether or not a mutation or LOH was present. p53 protein immunostaining was negative in almost all adenomas but positive in 86% of invasive carcinomas with a p53 mutation. The authors suggested that changes in both p53 alleles through mutation and LOH, leading to abnormal protein accumulation, are involved in the conversion of adenoma to early carcinoma.

subject: Houlston et al. (1992)
object: Houlston et al. (1992) performed complex segregation analysis of a published series of consecutive pedigrees ascertained through patients treated for colorectal cancer. The analysis favored a dominant gene or genes with a frequency of 0.006 and a lifetime penetrance of 0.63.

subject: Houlston et al. (1992)
object: Houlston et al. (1992) estimated that these dominant genes accounted for 81% of colorectal cancer in patients under 35 years of age, whereas by age 65 about 85% of cases were phenocopies.

subject: Ponz de Leon et al. (1992)
object: Ponz de Leon et al. (1992) performed classical segregation analysis on 605 families of colorectal carcinoma probands ascertained through the Cancer Registry of the Province of Modena, Italy. Of these, 28 were suspected HNPCC families and 577 were presumed non-HNPCC. Among the non-HNPCC families, both parents were affected in 11, one parent in 130 and neither parent in 436. In the suspected HNPCC families, segregation was compatible with dominant transmission of susceptibility to carcinoma.

subject: Ponz de Leon et al. (1992)
object: Ponz de Leon et al. (1992) found that in colorectal cancer families with one affected parent, the segregation frequency was almost exactly equal to that in families where both parents were normal. A model of dominant transmission of susceptibility through a major gene with greatly reduced penetrance in heterozygotes fitted the data acceptably.

subject: Laird et al. (1995)
object: Laird et al. (1995) studied the effects of reduced DNA methyltransferase activity on ApcMin-induced intestinal neoplasia in mice. They combined heterozygosity for the DNA methyltransferase gene with a weekly dose of the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor 5-aza-deoxycytidine. In these treated heterozygous Min mice, the average number of intestinal adenomas fell from 113 in control mice to only 2. The authors concluded that DNA methyltransferase activity contributes substantially to tumor development in this model, and that their results argue against an oncogenic effect of DNA hypomethylation.

subject: Laird et al. (1995)
object: Laird et al. (1995) stated that their findings in ApcMin mice are consistent with DNA methyltransferase playing a role in generating the C-to-T transitions that occur at high frequency in human colorectal tumors.

subject: Thomas (1995)
object: Thomas (1995) proposed that genomic imprinting could act as a surveillance mechanism for chromosome loss. Losing the transcriptionally active homologue would change gene expression, and this change could be detected. Thomas (1995) suggested that this surveillance might protect against cancer and allow monosomic and trisomic fetuses to be eliminated early.

subject: Lengauer et al. (1997)
object: Lengauer et al. (1997) found that colorectal tumors without microsatellite instability had a striking defect in chromosome segregation, with chromosomes gained or lost at rates above 10(-2) per chromosome per generation. This chromosomal instability reflected an ongoing cellular defect that lasted throughout the lifetime of the tumor cell and was not simply related to chromosome number.

subject: Lengauer et al. (1997)
object: Lengauer et al. (1997) reported that microsatellite instability is a recessive trait, while chromosomal instability appeared to be dominant. They concluded that persistent genetic instability may be critical for the development of all colorectal cancers and that such instability can arise through 2 distinct pathways.

subject: Jones and Gonzalgo (1997)
object: Jones and Gonzalgo (1997) asked whether altered DNA methylation and genome instability might be a new pathway to cancer.

subject: Lengauer et al. (1997)
object: Lengauer et al. (1997) found striking differences in the expression of exogenously introduced retroviral genes among colorectal cancer cell lines. Loss of expression was associated with DNA methylation and could be reversed by the demethylating agent 5-azacytidine. Because genetic instability correlated strikingly with methylation capacity, the authors suggested that methylation abnormalities may play a role in chromosome segregation in cancer cells.

subject: Sarraf et al. (1999)
object: Sarraf et al. (1999) identified 4 somatic PPAR-gamma (PPARG) mutations among 55 sporadic colon cancers: 1 nonsense, 1 frameshift, and 2 missense mutations. Each mutation greatly impaired the function of the protein. The authors concluded that colon cancer in humans is associated with loss-of-function mutations in PPARG.

subject: Sarraf et al. (1999)
object: In a sporadic colon cancer, Sarraf et al. (1999) identified a somatic frameshift mutation in PPARG, c.472delA, which results in deletion of the entire ligand-binding domain.

subject: PPARG c.472dela
object: PPARG

subject: Sarraf et al. (1999)
object: In a sporadic colon cancer, Sarraf et al. (1999) identified a somatic missense mutation in PPARG, Q286P. The mutant kept the ligand-binding domain but could not activate transcription because it failed to bind ligands.

subject: PPARG p.Q286P
object: PPARG

subject: Sarraf et al. (1999)
object: In a sporadic colon cancer, Sarraf et al. (1999) identified a somatic nonsense mutation in PPARG, K319X. The truncated protein kept part of the ligand-binding domain but could not activate transcription because it failed to bind ligands.

subject: PPARG p.K319*
object: PPARG

subject: Sarraf et al. (1999)
object: In a sporadic colon cancer, Sarraf et al. (1999) identified a somatic missense mutation in PPARG, R288H. The mutant responded normally to synthetic ligands but showed greatly decreased transcription and ligand binding when exposed to natural ligands.

subject: PPARG p.R288H
object: PPARG

subject: Baron et al. (1999)
object: Baron et al. (1999) conducted a randomized, double-blind trial in which 930 subjects (mean age 61 years; 72% men) with a recent history of colorectal adenomas received calcium carbonate (3 g, i.e. 1200 mg elemental calcium, daily) or placebo, with follow-up colonoscopies 1 and 4 years after the qualifying examination. Among the 832 subjects who completed both follow-up examinations, at least 1 adenoma was diagnosed between the first and second follow-up endoscopies in 31% of the calcium group and 38% of the placebo group (adjusted risk ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.67-0.99; P = 0.04). The adjusted ratio of the average number of adenomas was 0.76, and the effect was independent of initial dietary fat and calcium intake. The authors concluded that calcium supplementation is associated with a significant though moderate reduction in the risk of recurrent colorectal adenomas.

subject: Wheeler et al. (2002)
object: Wheeler et al. (2002) analysed 21 non-familial, non-ampullary adenocarcinomas of the small intestine (14 male and 7 female patients; median age 64 years, range 21-85; 10 duodenal, 7 jejunal, 4 ileal). They found no mutations in the mutation cluster region of the APC gene. Only 1 tumour (5%) was replication error-positive at BAT26, and all tumours stained positive for hMLH1 and hMSH2. The authors suggested that adenocarcinoma of the small intestine may follow a different genetic pathway from colorectal cancer.

subject: Wheeler et al. (2002)
object: In the 21 small-intestinal adenocarcinomas, Wheeler et al. (2002) found increased nuclear beta-catenin expression with loss of membranous staining in 10 tumours (48%). Membrane expression of E-cadherin was absent or decreased in 8 tumours (38%), and strong nuclear p53 staining was seen in 5 tumours (24%). The authors suggested that abnormal E-cadherin and beta-catenin expression reflects an early alternative to APC in this pathway.

subject: Rajagopalan et al. (2002)
object: Rajagopalan et al. (2002) found that somatic BRAF mutations in colorectal cancers occurred only in tumors that did not carry KRAS mutations. They concluded that this gave genetic support for the idea that BRAF and KRAS mutations have equivalent effects in tumorigenesis.

subject: Rajagopalan et al. (2002)
object: Rajagopalan et al. (2002) reported that BRAF mutation in colorectal tumors was linked to the tumors' mismatch-repair status. The authors stated that this emphasizes the role of repair processes in shaping the mutation spectra of human cancer.

subject: Gruber et al. (2002)
object: Gruber et al. (2002) studied BLM heterozygosity in relation to the risk of colorectal cancer.

subject: Sandler et al. (2003)
object: Sandler et al. (2003) conducted a randomized, double-blind trial in which 635 patients with previous colorectal cancer received either 325 mg of aspirin per day or placebo. Among the 517 patients with at least one colonoscopy (median 12.8 months after randomization), one or more adenomas were found in 17% of the aspirin group and 27% of the placebo group (P = 0.004). The adjusted relative risk of any recurrent adenoma with aspirin was 0.65 (95% CI, 0.46-0.91), and time to detection of a first adenoma was longer with aspirin (hazard ratio 0.64). The authors concluded that daily aspirin use is associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of colorectal adenomas in patients with previous colorectal cancer.

subject: Baron et al. (2003)
object: Baron et al. (2003) performed a randomized, double-blind trial of aspirin as a chemopreventive agent in 1,121 patients with a recent history of histologically documented colorectal adenomas, assigned to placebo (372), 81 mg aspirin (377), or 325 mg aspirin (372) daily. Among the 1,084 patients (97%) with follow-up colonoscopy at least 1 year after randomization, the incidence of 1 or more adenomas was 47% with placebo, 38% with 81 mg aspirin, and 45% with 325 mg aspirin (global P = 0.04); relative risks of any adenoma were 0.81 (95% CI, 0.69-0.96) for 81 mg and 0.96 (95% CI, 0.81-1.13) for 325 mg.

subject: Baron et al. (2003)
object: For advanced neoplasms (adenomas at least 1 cm or with tubulovillous or villous features, severe dysplasia, or invasive cancer), Baron et al. (2003) found relative risks of 0.59 (95% CI, 0.38-0.92) with 81 mg aspirin and 0.83 (95% CI, 0.55-1.23) with 325 mg aspirin compared with placebo. They concluded that low-dose aspirin has a moderate chemopreventive effect on adenomas in the large bowel.

subject: Cui et al. (2003)
object: Cui et al. (2003) noted that loss of imprinting (LOI) of the IGF2 gene, an epigenetic change, is found in the normal colonic mucosa of about 30% of colorectal cancer patients but in only 10% of healthy people.

subject: Cui et al. (2003)
object: In a pilot study of 172 patients seen at a colonoscopy clinic, Cui et al. (2003) found that IGF2 LOI in lymphocytes was associated with CRC risk. The adjusted odds ratio was 5.15 for patients with a positive family history (95% CI, 1.70-16.96; P = 0.002), 3.46 for patients with adenomas (95% CI, 1.14-11.37; P = 0.026), and 21.7 for patients with CRC (95% CI, 3.48-153.6; P = 0.0005). The authors suggested that LOI, which can be assayed with a DNA-based blood test, may be a valuable predictive marker of an individual's CRC risk.

subject: Bardelli et al. (2003)
object: Bardelli et al. (2003) performed a mutational analysis of the tyrosine kinome in colorectal cancers.

subject: Samuels et al. (2004)
object: Samuels et al. (2004) reported a high frequency of mutations in the PIK3CA gene in human cancers. Only the title was available, so the tumour types, the specific variants and the mutation frequencies are not known from this source.

subject: Fearnhead et al. (2004)
object: Fearnhead et al. (2004) screened germline DNA from 124 patients with 3 to 100 histologically proven synchronous or metachronous colorectal adenomas. They tested all patients for the APC variants I1307K and E1317Q and looked for variants in AXIN1, CTNNB1, MLH1, and MSH2. Thirty of the 124 patients (24.9%) carried potentially pathogenic germline variants, compared with 55 (about 12%) of 483 random controls. The authors said this highly significant difference suggested that many rare variants together contribute to inherited susceptibility to colorectal adenomas.

subject: APC p.I1307K
object: APC

subject: APC p.E1317Q
object: APC

subject: Fearnhead et al. (2004)
object: Fearnhead et al. (2004) noted that clear-cut Mendelian traits such as familial adenomatous polyposis and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer account for less than 4% of colorectal cancers. They noted that another 20% are thought to arise in people with a significant inherited multifactorial susceptibility that is not obviously familial. Using multiple colorectal adenomas as a model, the authors tested the hypothesis that rare variants account for this multifactorial inheritance.

subject: Batlle et al. (2005)
object: Batlle et al. (2005) found that most human colorectal cancers lose EphB receptor expression at the adenoma-carcinoma transition, even though Wnt signaling remains constitutively active. EphB receptors are Tcf4 target genes. Loss of EphB expression correlated strongly with degree of malignancy. The authors concluded that loss of EphB expression is a critical step in colorectal cancer progression.

subject: Batlle et al. (2005)
object: Batlle et al. (2005) found that reducing EphB activity in Apc(Min/+) mice accelerated tumorigenesis in the colon and rectum and led to the formation of aggressive adenocarcinomas.

subject: Parsons et al. (2005)
object: Parsons et al. (2005) analyzed human colorectal cancers for mutations in 340 serine/threonine kinases. They found mutations in 8 genes, including 3 members of the phosphatidylinositol-3-OH kinase (PI3K) pathway. The authors suggested that this mutational activation of a key cell-signaling pathway may provide new targets for therapeutic intervention.

subject: Greaves et al. (2006)
object: Greaves et al. (2006) showed that nononcogenic mitochondrial DNA mutations established in colonic crypt stem cells spread through the normal human colon by crypt fission: mutated cytochrome c oxidase-deficient crypts undergoing fission and neighboring mutated crypts shared the same mitochondrial genotype, which differed from adjacent cytochrome c oxidase-positive crypts; mutated crypts were clustered throughout the colon, and patches of cytochrome c oxidase-deficient crypts increased in size with age. The authors suggested this may have implications for the growth and spread of colorectal neoplasms.

subject: Boraska Jelavić et al. (2006)
object: Boraska Jelavić et al. (2006) genotyped the TLR2 GT microsatellite polymorphism and the TLR2 Arg753Gln polymorphism in 89 Croatian patients with sporadic colorectal cancer and 88 age- and sex-matched controls. In patients, TLR2 GT microsatellite alleles with 20 and 21 GT repeats were less frequent (p = 0.0044 and p = 0.001, respectively) and the allele with 31 GT repeats was more frequent (p = 0.0147). The authors reported an association of the TLR2 GT microsatellite polymorphism with sporadic colorectal cancer.

subject: TLR2 TLR2 GT microsatelite polymorphism
object: TLR2

subject: Boraska Jelavić et al. (2006)
object: In the same case-control study of 89 Croatian sporadic colorectal cancer patients and 88 matched controls, Boraska Jelavić et al. (2006) found that the mutant Asp299Gly allele of TLR4 was slightly more frequent in patients (p = 0.0269), and reported an association of this polymorphism with sporadic colorectal cancer; TLR4 Thr399Ile was also genotyped.

subject: TLR4 p.D299G
object: TLR4

subject: Sjöblom et al. (2006)
object: Sjöblom et al. (2006) sequenced 13,023 well-annotated human protein-coding genes in 11 breast and 11 colorectal cancers. They found that individual tumors accumulated an average of about 90 mutant genes, but only a subset of these contributed to the neoplastic process. Using stringent criteria, they identified 189 genes (an average of 11 per tumor) that were mutated at significant frequency. Most of these genes were not previously known to be genetically altered in tumors and were predicted to affect functions including transcription, adhesion, and invasion.

subject: Forrest and Cavet (2007)
object: Forrest and Cavet (2007) commented on the cancer genome resequencing analysis of breast and colorectal cancers by Sjoblom et al. (2006). They stated that the earlier analysis used point probabilities when it should have used P values for the hypotheses being tested. When Forrest and Cavet (2007) reran the analysis method with exact P values, far fewer genes had mutation rates that reached statistical significance.

subject: Getz et al. (2007)
object: Getz et al. (2007) commented on the report by Sjoblom et al. of nearly 200 novel cancer genes said to have a 90% probability of involvement in colon or breast cancer. They raised two statistical concerns about that analysis and found that, once these were addressed, few genes with significantly elevated mutation rates remained. They concluded that more samples were needed to achieve sufficient power.

subject: Rubin and Green (2007)
object: Rubin and Green (2007) reanalyzed the somatic mutation data of Sjöblom et al. (2006) from breast and colorectal cancers using what they considered more appropriate statistical methods and background mutation rate assumptions. They concluded that few if any of the newly reported candidate cancer genes had significantly elevated mutation rates.

subject: Wood et al. (2007)
object: Wood et al. (2007) sequenced exons representing 20,857 transcripts from 18,191 RefSeq genes in DNA from 11 colorectal and 11 breast tumors. They concluded that the genomic landscapes of these cancers consist of a handful of commonly mutated gene 'mountains' and a much larger number of gene 'hills' mutated at low frequency. They described statistical and bioinformatic tools that may help identify mutations with a role in tumorigenesis.

subject: Wood et al. (2007)
object: Wood et al. (2007) stated that their findings have implications for understanding the nature and heterogeneity of human cancers and for using personal genomics for tumor diagnosis and therapy.

subject: Daley et al. (2008)
object: Daley et al. (2008) performed a genome-wide linkage scan of 194 kindreds with familial colorectal neoplasia from the colon neoplasia sibling study. Families were classified into 5 phenotypic subgroups (severe histopathology, oligopolyposis, young, colon/breast, and multiple cancer), and affected, unaffected, and discordant sib pairs were analyzed. Sib-pair linkage statistics and Haseman-Elston regression identified 19 linkage peaks, with notable results for chromosomes 1p31.1, 15q14-q22, 17p13.3, and 21.

subject: Daley et al. (2008)
object: Daley et al. (2008) found strong evidence for linkage at marker D1S1665 on chromosome 1p31.1 in the multiple-cancer subgroup of familial colorectal neoplasia families (p = 0.00007).

subject: Daley et al. (2008)
object: Daley et al. (2008) identified a linkage peak on chromosome 15q14-q22 in the full sample (p = 0.018) and in the oligopolyposis (p = 0.003) and young-onset (p = 0.0009) subgroups. This region includes the HMPS/CRAC1 locus associated with hereditary mixed polyposis syndrome in Ashkenazi families, and the authors provided evidence linking this region in families of European descent with oligopolyposis and/or young age at onset (51 years or younger).

subject: Daley et al. (2008)
object: In the colon/breast cancer subgroup, Daley et al. (2008) found linkage to BRCA2 and identified a second locus near D21S1437 on chromosome 21 segregating with, but distinct from, BRCA2. Linkage to 17p13.3 at marker D17S1308 in the breast/colon subgroup identified HIC1 as a candidate gene.

subject: Alhopuro et al. (2008)
object: Alhopuro et al. (2008) screened patients with colorectal cancer, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and juvenile polyposis for MYH11 mutations. They found somatic protein-elongating frameshift mutations in MYH11 in 55% of colorectal cancers with microsatellite instability. They also found 2 somatic missense mutations, R501L and K1044N, in one microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer.

subject: MYH11 p.R501L
object: MYH11

subject: MYH11 p.K1044N
object: MYH11

subject: Alhopuro et al. (2008)
object: Alhopuro et al. (2008) tested the R501L and K1044N missense mutations and the frameshift mutations in MYH11. All of them produced unregulated myosin molecules with constitutive motor activity, similar to the mutant myosin that causes the zebrafish meltdown phenotype. The authors suggested that unregulated MYH11 may affect cellular energy balance or disturb cell lineage decisions in tumor progenitor cells.

subject: McMurray et al. (2008)
object: McMurray et al. (2008) showed that a large proportion of genes controlled synergistically by loss-of-function p53 and Ras activation ('cooperation response genes') were critical to the malignant state of murine and human colon cells. In gene perturbation experiments, 14 of 24 cooperation response genes contributed to tumor formation, compared with only 1 of 14 perturbations of non-synergistically responding genes. The authors suggested that synergistic control of gene expression by oncogenic mutations is an underlying key to malignancy and provides a rationale for identifying intervention targets.

subject: Vilar and Gruber (2010)
object: Vilar and Gruber (2010) reviewed microsatellite instability (MSI) in colorectal cancer, noting that approximately 15% of colorectal cancers display MSI. This is due either to epigenetic silencing of MLH1 or to a germline mutation in one of the mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2. They stated that most MSI colorectal cancers are sporadic and caused by MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, whereas 2 to 3% of all colorectal cancers are caused by germline mismatch repair gene mutations (Lynch syndrome).

subject: Vilar and Gruber (2010)
object: Vilar and Gruber (2010) noted that population-based studies have reported MSI in 8 to 20% of colorectal cancers. MSI was more common in stage II (about 20%) than in stage III (about 12%) or stage IV (about 4%) tumors. They also noted that 2 small retrospective studies suggested a higher frequency of MSI tumors in African American (20-45%) and Egyptian (37%) populations.

subject: Vilar and Gruber (2010)
object: Vilar and Gruber (2010) summarized the clinical and pathological profile of MSI colorectal cancers. These tumors tend to be right-sided and diagnosed at lower pathological stages, with high histological grade, mucinous features, prominent tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, absence of dirty necrosis, and a Crohn-like host response. Sporadic MSI cases are generally diagnosed after age 70 years, whereas familial cases are diagnosed before age 50 years.

subject: Vilar and Gruber (2010)
object: Vilar and Gruber (2010) noted that BRAF mutations, mostly V600E in exon 15, are present in 10% of colorectal cancers and do not occur together with KRAS mutations. BRAF mutations are more frequent in sporadic MSI tumors with MLH1 hypermethylation than in hereditary (Lynch syndrome) cases. KRAS mutations, present in about 40% of primary colorectal tumors, are more frequent in microsatellite-stable tumors (those with chromosomal instability) than in MSI tumors.

subject: BRAF p.V600E
object: BRAF

subject: Vilar and Gruber (2010)
object: Vilar and Gruber (2010) noted that PI3K pathway genes are altered in about 40% of colorectal tumors. PIK3CA mutation rates were reported at 10 to 30%, and other genes in the pathway (PDK1, AKT2, PAK4, IRS2, INSRR, ERBB4, PTEN) were also mutated. PTEN was both mutated and frequently epigenetically silenced in MSI tumors.

subject: Vilar and Gruber (2010)
object: Vilar and Gruber (2010) described how MSI is detected using the Bethesda panel of 5 microsatellite markers (BAT25, BAT26, D5S346, D2S123, D17S250). Tumors are classified as MSI-high (2 or more unstable loci), MSI-low, or microsatellite stable. Immunohistochemistry for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 indicates which gene is most likely inactivated. Loss of MLH1 is typically accompanied by loss of PMS2, and MLH1 promoter methylation is typically accompanied by somatic BRAF V600E.

subject: Vilar and Gruber (2010)
object: Vilar and Gruber (2010) reviewed a meta-analysis of 32 studies with 7,642 cases, 1,277 of them MSI. It confirmed that MSI colorectal cancers have a better prognosis and spread less often to lymph nodes and distant sites than microsatellite-stable cancers. Data from 6 randomized trials (Sargent et al.) suggested that 5-FU-based adjuvant chemotherapy gives no benefit, and might even be harmful, in stage II MSI tumors. Evidence for a benefit from irinotecan in MSI tumors remained preliminary and conflicting.

subject: Vilar and Gruber (2010)
object: Vilar and Gruber (2010) noted that MSI colorectal cancers usually have a stable karyotype, unlike chromosomally unstable tumors. In mismatch repair-deficient tumors, frameshift mutations occur in coding microsatellites of more than 30 genes, including TGFBR2, IGF2R, BAX, MSH3, MSH6, MRE11A, and RAD50. MRE11A mutations are found in 70 to 85% of MSI tumors and may increase sensitivity to irinotecan.

subject: Neklason et al. (2010)
object: Neklason et al. (2010) described a large Utah kindred (K5275), identified through the Utah Population Database, with a statistical excess of colorectal cancer (familial standardized incidence ratio 12.4). The family showed no clinical or molecular features of known hereditary colon cancer syndromes. In the 4 generations studied, the average age at colon cancer diagnosis was 46 years and the average age at detection of the first adenoma was 49.5 years. Of 32 kindred members who had colonoscopy, 3 had CRC, 9 had adenomatous polyps, and 22 had no adenomas. No one had more than 5 adenomas. No affected member had advanced adenomas, but 2 of the 3 cancers (diagnosed at ages 42 and 35) were metastatic at diagnosis, which the authors took as a subtle suggestion that adenomas may advance rapidly to metastasis.

subject: Neklason et al. (2010)
object: In the K5275 kindred, Neklason et al. (2010) excluded Lynch syndrome because 2 colorectal cancers were microsatellite stable, and they found no evidence of polyposis syndromes. LOD scores were negative near the known familial colon cancer genes APC, MYH, CTNNB1, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, STK11, PTEN, and BMPR1A. One marker near SMAD4 was positive, but the other markers near SMAD4 gave negative LOD scores.

subject: Neklason et al. (2010)
object: Neklason et al. (2010) performed genomewide STR and SNP linkage scans of kindred K5275 and identified a single major locus on chromosome 13q that segregated with adenomatous polyps and colon cancer. Under an autosomal dominant model, the maximum 2-point LOD score was 2.43 at D13S251. Nonparametric analysis gave a maximum NPL score of 24.12 (LOD 2.99, p = 0.001) at D13S251. The nonrecombinant region spanned rs1870836 (13q22.2) to D13S265 (13q31.3), about 21 Mb containing 27 RefSeq genes.

subject: Neklason et al. (2010)
object: Neklason et al. (2010) sequenced 8 candidate cancer-related genes in the 13q linked region: KLF5, KLF12, LMO7, RNF219, SPRY2, GPC5, MYCBP2, and POU4F1. They found no unambiguously deleterious mutation. They did find polymorphisms that segregated with the phenotype, including SNPs in SPRY2, RNF219, LMO7, and KLF12 and a novel SNP in the POU4F1 promoter. Whether these SNPs were causative or in disequilibrium with the causal change could not be determined.

subject: Neklason et al. (2010)
object: Neklason et al. (2010) performed CGH on a metastatic colon cancer from an obligate carrier of the 13q haplotype (diagnosed at age 42). It showed duplication of most of 13q, plus losses typical of sporadic CRC (APC, TP53, DCC, SMAD4). In STR peak-ratio analysis, all 3 family cancers showed a copy number gain at 1 of 3 13q markers, whereas 2 adenomas showed no change. Because 13q is gained in 30 to 50% of CRCs and correlates with metastasis, the authors suggested that the locus may harbor a gain-of-function cancer progression gene.

subject: Ward et al. (2011)
object: Ward et al. (2011) screened 2 European-origin cohorts with sporadic colorectal adenocarcinoma and 2 age- and sex-matched control cohorts for the most common European PKHD1 mutation, T36M (107C-T). In the first study, they found 6 T36M heterozygotes among 1,601 controls (0.37%) and none among 1,842 colorectal cancer patients (p = 0.01). In the second study, they found 9 among 2,002 controls (0.45%) and 1 among 1,925 cancer patients (0.05%) (p = 0.022). Combined, T36M was found in 15 of 3,603 controls (0.42%) and 1 of 3,767 colorectal cancer patients (0.027%) (p = 0.0002; odds ratio 0.072). The authors concluded that heterozygous PKHD1 mutations are not a risk factor for colorectal cancer and are protective.

subject: PKHD1 c.107C>T / p.T36M
object: PKHD1

subject: Ward et al. (2011)
object: Ward et al. (2011) hypothesized that reduced fibrocystin activity could cause mitotic instability and centrosome amplification, so that premalignant cells have too much genomic instability to form aggressive tumors, which would explain the protective effect of the PKHD1 T36M mutation against colorectal carcinoma.

subject: Ward et al. (2011)
object: Ward et al. (2011) found that T36M made up 13.1% of PKHD1 mutations in a European ARPKD cohort. Using the T36M frequency in controls, they estimated the carrier frequency of all PKHD1 mutations in the European population at 3.2% (1 in 31), higher than the previous estimate of 1 in 70.

subject: Bass et al. (2011)
object: Bass et al. (2011) performed whole-genome sequencing on 9 primary colorectal adenocarcinomas and matched adjacent non-tumor tissue, at average coverages of 30.7x and 31.9x. The mutation rate was about 5.9 per Mb (range, 4.0-9.8), with a strong predilection for C-to-T transitions at CpG sites. KRAS, APC, and TP53 were mutated in 5, 7, and 6 tumors, respectively, and scored as significantly recurrent.

subject: Bass et al. (2011)
object: Bass et al. (2011) found an average of 75 somatic rearrangements per tumor (range, 5-182) across 9 colorectal cancer genomes. Three tumors showed clustered networks of balanced interchromosomal translocations between pairs of chromosomes, including chromosomes 8 and 20 in one tumor and chromosomes 5 and 11 in another. The authors described these as a variant of the chromothripsis pattern. They also found small deletions that removed the first exon of EGFR and the 3-prime section of PTEN.

subject: Bass et al. (2011)
object: Bass et al. (2011) identified 11 rearrangements across 9 colorectal cancer genomes that were predicted to produce in-frame fusions. One of these joined the first 3 exons of VTI1A to exon 4 of the adjacent TCF7L2 gene on chromosome 10, caused by an approximately 540-kb deletion. Screening cDNA from 97 primary colorectal cancers found in-frame VTI1A-TCF7L2 fusions in 3 tumors (3%). The fusion protein lacks the N-terminal beta-catenin-binding domain of TCF4. All 3 fusion-positive tumors also carried APC alterations.

subject: TCF7L2 VTI1A exon 3 to TCF7L2 exon 4 fusion
object: TCF7L2

subject: Bass et al. (2011)
object: Bass et al. (2011) found a point mutation in TCF7L2 in one colorectal tumor that affected the splice site at the 3-prime end of exon 10, the exon encoding the HMG-box DNA-binding domain. The authors considered this mutation likely deleterious.

subject: TCF7L2 splice-site mutation at 3' end of exon 10
object: TCF7L2

subject: Bass et al. (2011)
object: Bass et al. (2011) showed that the colorectal cancer cell line NCI-H508 carries a deletion producing an in-frame fusion of VTI1A exon 2 to TCF7L2 exon 5. Knocking down the fusion transcript with shRNA sharply reduced anchorage-independent growth of NCI-H508 cells but not of the fusion-negative DLD-1 cells. NCI-H508 also depended on beta-catenin. The authors suggested that VTI1A-TCF7L2 is expressed in the setting of activated beta-catenin.

subject: Dorard et al. (2011)
object: Dorard et al. (2011) identified a mutant of HSP110, HSP110-delta-E9, in colorectal cancers with microsatellite instability (MSI CRC). The mutant was generated from an aberrantly spliced mRNA and lacked the HSP110 substrate-binding domain. It was expressed at variable levels in almost all MSI CRC cell lines and primary tumors tested.

subject: HSP110 HSP110ΔE9
object: HSP110

subject: Dorard et al. (2011)
object: Dorard et al. (2011) found that HSP110-delta-E9 disrupted the normal cellular localization of HSP110 and its interaction with other HSPs. In a dominant-negative manner, it abolished the chaperone activity and antiapoptotic function of HSP110. Overexpression of HSP110-delta-E9 made cells more sensitive to oxaliplatin and 5-fluorouracil.

subject: Dorard et al. (2011)
object: Dorard et al. (2011) found that survival and response to chemotherapy in patients with MSI colorectal cancer were associated with the level of HSP110-delta-E9 expression in the tumor. They suggested that HSP110 may be a major determinant of both prognosis and treatment response in colorectal cancer.

subject: Montagut et al. (2012)
object: Montagut et al. (2012) identified an acquired somatic mutation in the EGFR ectodomain, S492R, in 2 of 10 colorectal cancer patients with disease progression after cetuximab treatment. The mutation prevented cetuximab binding and conferred resistance to cetuximab, whereas cells with the mutation retained binding to and were growth inhibited by panitumumab.

subject: EGFR p.S492R
object: EGFR

subject: Montagut et al. (2012)
object: Montagut et al. (2012) reported that a colorectal cancer patient with cetuximab resistance whose tumor harbored the acquired EGFR S492R mutation responded to treatment with panitumumab.

subject: Prahallad et al. (2012)
object: Prahallad et al. (2012) found that colon cancers with the BRAF V600E mutation respond poorly to the BRAF inhibitor PLX4032 (vemurafenib). In an RNA-interference screen of kinases in human cells, blocking EGFR was strongly synergistic with BRAF V600E inhibition. In multiple BRAF V600E-mutant colon cancers, inhibiting EGFR with cetuximab, gefitinib, or erlotinib was strongly synergistic with BRAF V600E inhibition both in vitro and in vivo. The authors suggested that BRAF V600E-mutant colon cancers, about 8 to 10% of all colon cancers, might benefit from combined BRAF and EGFR inhibitors.

subject: Prahallad et al. (2012)
object: Prahallad et al. (2012) found that inhibiting BRAF V600E in colon cancer cells caused rapid feedback activation of EGFR, which allowed the cells to keep proliferating despite the BRAF inhibition. Melanoma cells express low levels of EGFR and were not subject to this feedback. Ectopic expression of EGFR in melanoma cells was sufficient to cause resistance to PLX4032.

subject: Diaz et al. (2012)
object: Diaz et al. (2012) retrospectively analyzed serial serum samples from 28 patients with chemorefractory metastatic colorectal cancer receiving panitumumab monotherapy for circulating mutant KRAS DNA. Of 24 patients whose tumors were initially KRAS wildtype, 9 (38%) developed detectable KRAS codon 12/13 mutations in serum during therapy, 3 of whom developed multiple different KRAS mutations (2 in one patient and 4 in two others); none developed BRAF mutations. The authors suggested that emergence of KRAS mutations is a mediator of acquired resistance to EGFR blockade and can be detected noninvasively.

subject: Diaz et al. (2012)
object: Diaz et al. (2012) found that in KRAS-wildtype metastatic colorectal cancer patients treated with panitumumab, the appearance of circulating KRAS mutations was very consistent, generally occurring 5 to 6 months after treatment initiation (23 +/- 5 weeks), and mutant KRAS was detected before radiographic progression in 3 of 9 cases with an average lead time of 21 weeks. Circulating tumor DNA levels generally paralleled CEA. Progression-free and overall survival did not differ significantly between those who did and did not develop secondary KRAS mutations.

subject: Diaz et al. (2012)
object: Using mathematical modeling of serial circulating tumor DNA data, Diaz et al. (2012) concluded that KRAS mutations conferring resistance to panitumumab were present in expanded subclones before therapy began, and estimated that about 42 nucleotides (in perhaps about 10 genes) could confer resistance, with each large metastatic lesion expected to harbor hundreds to thousands of resistant cells before treatment. They suggested that resistance is a 'fait accompli' and that combination therapies targeting at least two pathways would be required for longer remissions.

subject: Diaz et al. (2012)
object: Diaz et al. (2012) found that in 3 of 4 metastatic colorectal cancer patients with KRAS-mutant archival tumors, the identical KRAS mutation was detectable in pretreatment serum, whereas no KRAS mutations were detected in pretreatment serum of patients with KRAS-wildtype tumors, supporting circulating tumor DNA as a 'liquid biopsy.'

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) performed a genome-scale analysis of 276 colorectal carcinoma samples, including exome sequencing of 224 tumor-normal pairs, DNA copy number, promoter methylation, and mRNA and microRNA expression, with low-depth whole-genome sequencing of 97 samples. Overall, 16% of tumors were hypermutated; three-quarters of these had high microsatellite instability (MSI-H), usually with hypermethylation and MLH1 silencing, and one-quarter had somatic mismatch-repair gene and POLE mutations.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: Among 30 hypermutated tumors with complete data, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found that 23 (77%) were MSI-H, including 19 with MLH1 methylation (17 with CIMP); the remaining 7, including the 6 with the highest mutation rates, lacked MSI-H, CIMP, or MLH1 methylation but usually had somatic mutations in mismatch-repair genes or POLE aberrations.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) identified 24 significantly mutated genes; among non-hypermutated tumors the most frequently mutated were APC, TP53, KRAS, PIK3CA, FBXW7, SMAD4, TCF7L2, and NRAS, with CTNNB1, SMAD2, FAM123B (WTX), and SOX9 also frequently mutated. All 9 SOX9 mutant alleles in non-hypermutated tumors were frameshift or nonsense, and ATM and ARID1A had a disproportionate number of frameshift or nonsense mutations.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: In hypermutated tumors, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found frequent mutations in ACVR2A, APC, TGFBR2, MSH3, MSH6, SLC9A9, and TCF7L2, along with mostly BRAF V600E mutations; TP53 (60% vs 20%) and APC (81% vs 51%) were significantly less frequently mutated in hypermutated than non-hypermutated tumors, indicating that the two groups progress through different sequences of genetic events.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found that, excluding hypermutated cancers, colon and rectal carcinomas had indistinguishable patterns of copy number, CIMP, mRNA, and miRNA changes; however, tumors from the right/ascending colon were more likely to be hypermethylated and hypermutated, with three-quarters of hypermutated samples from the right colon.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: Among 257 tumors profiled by SNP arrays, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found deletion of 18p and 18q (including SMAD4) in 66% and of 17p and 17q (including TP53) in 56%, 28 recurrent deletion peaks, and 17 regions of focal amplification, including an ERBB2-containing amplicon at 17q21.1 in 4% of tumors and a 100- to 150-kb amplification at 11p15.5 in 7% of tumors that included IGF2 and miR-483, whose expression was elevated.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found that IGF2 overexpression (by amplification or otherwise) was nearly mutually exclusive with PI3K pathway-activating events (PIK3CA, PIK3R1, PTEN), and that high IRS2 expression was mutually exclusive with IGF2 overexpression and PI3K pathway mutations, strongly suggesting that the IGF2-IGF1R-IRS2 axis signals to PI3K in CRC.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: By low-pass whole-genome sequencing of 97 tumors, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) identified 3 cases in which the first 2 exons of NAV2 on chromosome 11 were fused to the 3-prime coding portion of TCF7L1 on chromosome 2, with the predicted fusion protein lacking the TCF3 beta-catenin-binding domain; 21 translocations involving TTC28 predicted its inactivation.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: In integrated analysis of 195 tumors, the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found WNT signaling altered in 93% of tumors, including biallelic APC inactivation or activating CTNNB1 mutations in about 80%, with FZD10 overexpressed in about 17%; 55% of non-hypermutated tumors had KRAS, NRAS, or BRAF alterations; TGF-beta pathway alterations occurred in 27% of non-hypermutated and 87% of hypermutated tumors; and TP53 was altered in 59% of non-hypermutated cases. PARADIGM analysis showed changes in MYC transcriptional targets in nearly 100% of tumors, suggesting an important role for MYC.

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found mutations or amplifications of ERBB family genes in 13% of non-hypermutated and 53% of hypermutated cases, including recurrent ERBB2 V842I and ERBB3 V104M mutations in 4 and 2 non-hypermutated cases, respectively, and suggested these be evaluated as predictors of response to ERBB-targeted agents.

subject: ERBB2 p.V842I
object: ERBB2

subject: ERBB3 p.V104M
object: ERBB3

subject: Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012)
object: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012) found molecular signatures associated with tumor aggressiveness, including somatic mutations in APC, TP53, PIK3CA, BRAF, and FBXW7; FBXW7 mutations (38 cases) and distant metastasis (32 cases) never co-occurred.

subject: Seshagiri et al. (2012)
object: Seshagiri et al. (2012) sequenced the exomes of 72 primary colon tumour-normal pairs (15 MSI, 57 MSS) and also analysed RNA-seq, SNP-array and whole-genome data. They identified 36,303 protein-altering somatic changes. In MSS tumours they found 23 significantly mutated genes. These included known genes (KRAS, APC, TP53, SMAD4, FBXW7, PIK3CA) and new ones such as the checkpoint kinase gene ATM. They also found new recurrent mutations in TCF7L2, in TET2 and TET3, and in ERBB3.

subject: Seshagiri et al. (2012)
object: Seshagiri et al. (2012) found TCF12 mutations in 5 MSI colon tumours. Three of the 5 mutations hit a hotspot at Arg603 in the helix-loop-helix domain, and the authors stated that these probably abolish DNA binding. ERBB3 was mutated in 6 of 72 tumours (8%), and all three TET genes (TET1, TET2, TET3) were mutated.

subject: TCF12 Arg 603 hotspot
object: TCF12

subject: Seshagiri et al. (2012)
object: In 74 tumour-normal pairs, Seshagiri et al. (2012) found IGF2 overexpression in 8 of 68 colon tumours (12%), and 7 of these 8 had focal amplification of the IGF2 locus. They also found KRAS amplification (10 of 74) and MYC amplification (17 of 74). Deletions involved FHIT (22 of 74), APC, PTEN and SMAD3. Chromosome 18q (carrying SMAD4 and SMAD2) was frequently lost and chromosome 20q was frequently gained.

subject: Seshagiri et al. (2012)
object: Using RNA-seq, Seshagiri et al. (2012) found a recurrent EIF3E(exon 1)-RSPO2(exon 2) fusion in 2 of 68 MSS colon tumours (3%). The fusion is expected to produce functional RSPO2 driven by the EIF3E promoter. Whole-genome sequencing showed a 158-kb deletion in one tumour and a 113-kb deletion in the other, each placing EIF3E exon 1 next to the 5-prime end of RSPO2. RSPO2 expression was elevated in the fusion-positive tumours.

subject: RSPO2 EIF3E(e1)–RSPO2(e2) fusion
object: RSPO2

subject: Seshagiri et al. (2012)
object: Seshagiri et al. (2012) found PTPRK-RSPO3 fusions in 5 of 68 colon tumours (8%), caused by simple or complex inversions on chromosome 6q. In 4 tumours the in-frame PTPRK(e1)-RSPO3(e2) fusion keeps the entire RSPO3 coding sequence but uses the PTPRK secretion signal in place of RSPO3's own. In 1 tumour the in-frame PTPRK(e7)-RSPO3(e2) fusion encodes a protein of about 70 kD made of PTPRK amino acids 1-387 joined to RSPO3 amino acids 34-272.

subject: RSPO3 PTPRK(e1)–RSPO3(e2)
object: RSPO3

subject: RSPO3 PTPRK(e7)–RSPO3(e2)
object: RSPO3

subject: Seshagiri et al. (2012)
object: Seshagiri et al. (2012) found that the RSPO2 and RSPO3 fusions were mutually exclusive with each other. The fusions occurred in tumours without APC mutation or copy loss (P = 0.038), except for one RSPO2-fusion tumour with a single APC allele, and they were also mutually exclusive with CTNNB1 mutations. Every fusion-positive tumour carried a KRAS or BRAF mutation. Fusion-positive tumours showed upregulation of Wnt target genes similar to APC-mutant tumours, which the authors suggested means the fusions act analogously to APC mutations.

subject: Seshagiri et al. (2012)
object: Seshagiri et al. (2012) expressed the RSPO fusion constructs in 293T cells and showed that the fusion proteins were secreted. In a TOPbrite luciferase reporter assay, conditioned media containing the fusion proteins activated Wnt signalling, and this effect was further potentiated by added Wnt. The same activity was seen in HT-29 colon cancer cells. The authors concluded that R-spondins probably act as drivers in human colorectal cancer.

subject: Seshagiri et al. (2012)
object: Seshagiri et al. (2012) reported that Rspo2 was a top candidate cancer gene in Sleeping Beauty transposon mutagenesis screens in mouse models of colorectal cancer. In these mouse tumours, transposon insertions in Apc and in Rspo2 were mostly mutually exclusive. One tumour with an insertion near the Rspo2 transcription start site had about 20-fold higher Rspo2 mRNA than adjacent normal tissue.

subject: Schweiger et al. (2013)
object: In a review, Schweiger et al. (2013) described colorectal cancer as a complex disease with several layers, involving both the genome and the epigenome, with direct effects on gene and microRNA expression signatures. They noted that many tumor-suppressor genes and oncogenes are frequently mutated in colorectal cancer and might drive the malignant transformation.

subject: Douillard et al. (2013)
object: In a prospective-retrospective analysis of the PRIME trial, Douillard et al. (2013) tested tumors from 639 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer that had no KRAS exon 2 mutations. The tumors were tested for mutations in KRAS exons 3 and 4, NRAS exons 2, 3, and 4, and BRAF exon 15. A total of 108 patients (17%) with nonmutated KRAS exon 2 had other RAS mutations. These mutations were associated with inferior progression-free and overall survival with panitumumab-FOLFOX4, consistent with findings in patients with KRAS exon 2 mutations.

subject: Douillard et al. (2013)
object: Douillard et al. (2013) found that among 512 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer without RAS mutations, panitumumab-FOLFOX4 improved progression-free survival compared with FOLFOX4 alone (10.1 vs 7.9 months; hazard ratio 0.72; P = 0.004). It also improved overall survival (26.0 vs 20.2 months; hazard ratio 0.78; P = 0.04). The authors concluded that additional RAS mutations predicted a lack of response to panitumumab-FOLFOX4.

subject: Douillard et al. (2013)
object: Douillard et al. (2013) found that BRAF mutations were a negative prognostic factor in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer.

subject: Seguí et al. (2015)
object: Seguí et al. (2015) performed exome sequencing on 3 members of a family with colorectal cancer that met the Amsterdam criteria for hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer and had mismatch repair-proficient tumors. All 3 carried a nonsense variant in FAN1, which encodes a nuclease involved in DNA interstrand cross-link repair.

subject: Seguí et al. (2015)
object: Seguí et al. (2015) sequenced FAN1 in 176 additional families with a history of colorectal cancer and performed in vitro functional analyses of the mutant FAN1 proteins found. FAN1 mutations were detected in about 3% of families that met the Amsterdam criteria and had mismatch repair-proficient cancers with no previously associated mutations. The authors concluded that these findings link colorectal cancer predisposition to the Fanconi anemia DNA repair pathway.
